Subject: Pricing metrics: tokens vs characters vs requests — recap + next steps

Hi Anya — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap so we’re all aligned and a short list of next steps to unblock a clean pricing proposal.

TL;DR from our discussion
- TaxoSolutions rough footprint: ~250M tokens/month (peak).
- Workload mix: ~80% embeddings for semantic search, ~20% text generation for summaries and customer-facing snippets.
- Billability ask: you want guidance on unit economics and a target $/1M tokens to fit your procurement budget (you mentioned an initial target around $10k/month).

What caused the confusion on the call (summary)
- Tokens vs characters: internal devs were quoting character counts from the UI; our API billing is token-based. Tokenization typically compresses characters (on average ~3.5–4 characters per token for English), so character counts will under/over-estimate billed tokens depending on language/punctuation.
- Requests vs tokens: requests = number of API calls; billing unit is tokens (input + output combined). High request volume with small payloads can still be cheap if token count per request is low, but many small requests increase overhead/latency.
- Prompt caching vs billed tokens: caching reduces compute and effectively reduces billed tokens only when a cache hit returns a previously generated response without recomputing. If a call hits the prefix/KV cache and we serve from cache, that request is often not billed for full token compute. However, partial-cache situations (different suffixes) still bill for the new tokens. We'll show examples below.

Actionable items we agreed to produce (next steps):
1) You: share 3 representative API logs (an embedding call, a short generation call, a long generation call) — we’ll tokenize them and return exact billed-token estimates.
2) Us (Jasmine + Karthik): produce a back-of-envelope unit economics table showing: tokens/month -> estimated $/month at three price bands and an explicit $/1M tokens figure.
3) Us: send a short explainer (single-page) that maps characters -> tokens -> billed tokens and includes caching examples.
4) Logistics: schedule a 30-minute follow-up with your procurement team to walk budget numbers and SOW items.

Requested clarifications from Taxo on the call:
- Confirm the 250M tokens/month is a good peak estimate (or give a range).
- Confirm whether embeddings are batched in large bulk jobs (affects batching/cost).
- Procurement preferred term length and any required PO cadence.

I’m attaching a quick pricing cheatsheet and a very rough SOW draft to start the procurement thread.

Attachments: pricing-cheatsheet.xlsx (attachment_stub), SOW-draft-v1.pdf (attachment_stub)

Thanks — I’ll pick this up with Karthik and loop finance if we need a modeled quote for your mid-year ramp.

Best,
Jasmine
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Great summary, Jasmine. A couple of technical clarifications you can forward to Anya to make procurement comfortable:

- Tokenization rule of thumb: ~3.7 characters/token for English text in our models (so 1M characters ≈ 270k tokens). This is very rough — languages with long compound words or lots of punctuation vary. We will tokenize their actual sample logs for precise numbers.

- Billing model: Redwood invoices on tokens (input + output). Requests (# of API calls) are not a billing unit, but they do influence latency considerations and possible discounts (volume-based).

- Caching behavior (short version for procurement):
  * Full cache hit (exact prefix & stored response returned): typically not billed at token-level compute — it bypasses the model execution. It may still incur a small request handling charge in large enterprise billing scenarios (negligible for token-heavy workloads; we’ll flag if that’s relevant).
  * Partial/approx match: billed for the new/generated tokens only.
  * Embeddings: we cache identical vectors to avoid recompute where appropriate; duplicates are not billed multiple times when the same embedding request repeats and a cache hit returns the stored vector.

- Example (quick calc): if your generation call averages 120 tokens output + 30 token input = 150 tokens/call. At 20% of 250M tokens (50M tokens/month for generation), that’s ~333k calls/month. If your budget is $10k/month, that implies ~ $10k / (250 * 1M tokens) = $40 / 1M tokens — but that simple math looks off because it doesn't account for the mix. We should produce a proper table that maps the mixed workload to $/1M effective price.

I’ll run a couple of modeled rows and attach to the cheatsheet. Suggest we book the follow-up for Thursday so we can share the table live.

-Karthik
